_comment: SHARED FIXTURE - one answer key for the queue subsystem, all four frameworks.
ADR-0024: the developer writes against the CONTRACT, never the PROVIDER.
Swapping file for rabbitmq, kafka or mongodb changes ONE env var and NOTHING
ELSE. Identical application code, identical OBSERVABLE outcome.
These are INVARIANTS, not a bug list. Eleven defects were measured in this
subsystem on 2026-08-01; each one is an instance of one of the six rules
below being broken. Stating the rules is what stops the twelfth.
Queues have the most open findings of any subsystem AND no fixture - which is
the whole correlation this file exists to break. Every subsystem that already
has a fixture (dispatch, health, dotenv, write-path) is one where drift stopped
HOW THIS IS CHECKED: scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py asserts that every
invariant naming a suite+cases has those cases present in all four frameworks.
An invariant with an empty 'cases' list is OWED - declared and not yet proven.
Owed is reported loudly and does not fail the build; a case that was named and
has since disappeared DOES fail, because that is a test someone deleted.

invariants.rule: Every public Queue method resolves and runs on EVERY backend the framework OFFERS. No method may be a fatal error, a NoMethodError, or an undefined method. A backend the framework deliberately does NOT offer must refuse by name at construction (ADR-0022 decision 8), which is a documented refusal rather than a severed upgrade path.
invariants.why: MEASURED 2026-08-03 across every framework and backend. PHP failed()/deadLetters()/retry()/retryFailed() were a FATAL 'Call to undefined method' on rabbitmq AND kafka, because the QueueBackend INTERFACE never declared them while Queue called them on everything. Ruby queue.size raised NoMethodError on kafka. Python clear() raised AttributeError on mongodb - the only one of that adapter's six _collection users that forgot to connect first. A separate PHP defect surfaced from the test itself: a failed broker connect stored FALSE in the socket while ensureConnected() only reconnects on null, so every later call did fwrite(false, ...) and died with a TypeError. CORRECTION to the original wording of this invariant: Node's rabbitmq/kafka throw-at-construction was listed here as a violation. It is NOT - ADR-0022 decision 8 chose it deliberately over documenting an at-most-once footgun, and records it as a HOLDING POSITION pending a persistent connection. The fixture was wrong, not the code.
cases: every public queue method resolves on every backend
a backend that cannot answer a question refuses by name instead of lying
a supported method returns a real answer rather than a refusal
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-03, against a live MongoDB, RabbitMQ and Kafka. PHP: failed(), deadLetters() and retryFailed() are now DECLARED ON THE QueueBackend INTERFACE, so the type system enforces this invariant for them permanently, and the two brokers implement them as refusals naming the backend and the method - not as empty lists, which would claim nothing has failed (ADR-0022 decision 7). PHP also stopped storing FALSE in a broker socket after a failed connect. Ruby gained kafka size() -> 0, the answer ADR-0022 decision 5 already records and which Python and PHP already gave. Python's mongodb clear() now connects first. Node needed no code change: its broker refusal is ADR-0022 decision 8. Each test exercises every method in TWO modes - a FRESH queue per method and one SHARED across them - because they catch different bugs: fresh found Python's unconnected clear(), shared found PHP's dead socket. The first version of the Python test used only the shared mode and PASSED with the fix reverted, which is why both modes are now mandatory. Mutation-proved in all four: removing PHP's interface declarations plus implementations, Ruby's kafka size, Python's ensure_connected, or the backend name from Node's refusal each kills exactly the dependent cases.

invariants.rule: Every operation acts on the CONFIGURED backend. No method may silently read or write the local file store when another backend is selected.
invariants.why: MEASURED: PHP clear() and purge() always hit the local FILE store whatever backend is configured; Node popBatch() and popById() always read the local file store even on mongodb. The call appears to succeed and operates on the wrong data - a silent wrong answer, which is the worst failure class because nothing surfaces it.
cases: clear acts on the configured backend not the local file store
pop by id claims the job from the configured backend
an operation the backend cannot perform refuses instead of silently using the file store
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-03 against a live MongoDB, RabbitMQ and Kafka. The measurement found MORE than this invariant originally recorded. Recorded: PHP clear()/purge() always hit the local FILE store, and Node popBatch()/popById() always read it. FOUND AS WELL: pop_by_id was broken in ALL FOUR - unanimous, which makes it a contract nobody had written down rather than four independent bugs - and Ruby's clear() was broken too. Each framework failed differently. Python: `if not isinstance(self._backend, LiteBackend): return None`, a silent no-op. PHP: clear()/purge() called liteBackend unconditionally and popById() returned null with the comment 'External backends don't support ID-based pop natively', which mongodb does. Ruby: MongoBackend had NEITHER clear nor find_by_id, and Queue guarded on respond_to?, so both returned 0/nil. Node: both read the local file store on every backend. FIXED: mongodb now implements clear, purge and pop-by-id everywhere (claiming one document by id exactly as the head claim does, so a crashed consumer's job is still reclaimed); the brokers RAISE naming the backend and the operation, because neither can address a single message by id nor purge by job status; Node's popBatch loops the atomic pop(). PHP additionally gained clear/purge/popById on the QueueBackend INTERFACE, so the type system enforces the routing, and LiteBackend::clear now returns its count. Mutation-proved in all four: restoring each fall-through kills exactly the dependent case.

invariants.rule: job.fail() reaches the backend on every provider, and a job past max_retries becomes observable through dead_letters() on every provider. A dead-letter handler written locally must find the same jobs after deploying onto a broker.
invariants.why: MEASURED: on Ruby rabbitmq/kafka the whole failure lifecycle silently no-ops - job.fail() never reaches the backend and dead_letters() is always empty. A developer tests retry-and-dead-letter locally on file, ships it, and the dead-letter queue is permanently empty in production with no error anywhere.
cases: a failed job under max retries is retried rather than dead lettered
a job past max retries becomes a dead letter
a dead letter carries the attempt count and the failure reason
a completed job never appears in dead letters
reading dead letters does not consume them
failing a job reaches the configured backend and not just local memory
a backend that cannot enumerate retryable failures refuses by name
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04, against a live MongoDB and a live RabbitMQ. The lifecycle cases are PARAMETRISED over file AND mongodb because the equality of the two IS the invariant. MEASURED defects, all silent: mongodb failed() queried status="failed", which the retryable path never writes (it re-queues as "pending"), so it returned [] forever in python, node AND ruby - and ruby had no mongo failed() at all; mongo dead letters lost the attempt count and the error text; ruby's job.fail() NEVER REACHED rabbitmq or kafka because Job#fail was guarded by respond_to?(:fail) and neither broker defined one, so a failure was recorded in local memory while the delivery stayed unacked and no dead letter was written; ruby's five Queue methods each returned []/false/0 for a backend lacking the method, turning "cannot" into "nothing has failed"; max_retries never reached ruby's brokers so a job got 3 attempts on a broker and 2 on file; node's pop() and popById() returned external-backend jobs UNWRAPPED, so queue.pop().fail() was a TypeError on mongodb and worked on file. PHP's brokers REFUSED deadLetters() outright - a premise true of RabbitMQ's own dead-letter EXCHANGE but false of the <topic>.dead_letter queue Tina4 writes itself - and now answer it non-destructively (drain-and-republish on rabbitmq, offset rewind-and-restore on kafka), verified stable across three consecutive reads. failed()/retry_failed() still refuse on the brokers, correctly: a retryable failure is re-published to the MAIN topic where it cannot be told apart from pending work. Node satisfies the refusal half at CONSTRUCTION per ADR-0022 decision 8. MUTATION-PROVED in every framework, each mutation hitting exactly its own case. Recorded because it nearly fooled me: restoring ruby's respond_to? guard ALONE applied cleanly and proved NOTHING (12 examples, 0 failures), because the backend now HAS a fail method so the guard is inert - the original defect needed BOTH halves. A mutation that applies is not a mutation that reproduces. Kafka's lifecycle is written but NOT verified off-box: the lab broker advertises PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092, so any real client library dials localhost from another host; that verification belongs on the lab host.

invariants.rule: delay_seconds / delay is honoured on every backend. A job pushed with a delay is not visible to a consumer before that delay elapses.
invariants.why: MEASURED: delay is silently DROPPED on every non-file backend, in ALL FOUR frameworks. A scheduled job fires immediately in production and on time in development. This one is unanimous across the family, which makes it a contract that was never written down rather than four independent bugs.
cases: an undelayed job is visible immediately
a delayed job is not visible before its delay elapses
a delayed job becomes visible once its delay elapses
a backend that cannot delay refuses instead of dropping the delay
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-03, against a live MongoDB, RabbitMQ and Kafka. The fix splits by what each broker can actually do. MONGODB: implemented - a delayed job is stamped available_at in the future, which every dequeue already filtered on. Each framework dropped it in its OWN place, which is why the symptom was unanimous but the patch is not: python's adapter never passed delay_seconds to enqueue; PHP's Queue::push built a SEPARATE message array for the external-backend branch carrying neither priority nor delay_seconds, so the value never reached the backend at all; ruby never WROTE available_at and never FILTERED on it, so writing it alone would have changed nothing; node wrote delayUntil but put five conditions in ONE $or, making the reservation gate and the delay gate alternatives instead of requirements - a fresh delayed job has no availableAt, matched {$exists: false}, and was handed straight to a consumer. RABBITMQ and KAFKA: they RAISE naming the backend and the operation (invariant 6), because neither has a per-message delay - rabbitmq's delayed-message-exchange is a non-core plugin and the TTL+dead-letter workaround head-of-line blocks, and kafka reads a partition in offset order. Node satisfies this half by refusing those backends outright at construction (ADR-0022). Every case is mutation-proved: reverting each framework's fix kills exactly 'a delayed job is not visible before its delay elapses' and nothing else.

invariants.rule: priority orders delivery, and a job that is not yet available is not delivered, on every backend that claims to support them.
invariants.why: MEASURED: Ruby + mongodb ignores priority and job availability entirely on the read path; Node + mongodb builds an availability predicate as an OR that always matches, so both delay and retryBackoff are inert. An always-true predicate is indistinguishable from a working one until timing matters.
cases: a higher priority job is delivered before an older lower priority one
equal priority jobs are delivered oldest first
a backend that cannot prioritise refuses instead of dropping the priority
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-03, against a live MongoDB, RabbitMQ and Kafka. The AVAILABILITY half was closed first by delay-is-honoured-on-every-backend (Ruby never filtered on available_at; Node's predicate was an always-true OR) and is not re-tested here. PRIORITY was honoured only on the file backend: MEASURED before the fix, mongodb ignored it in PHP, Ruby AND Node, and every broker ignored it in all four. Each framework lost it somewhere different. PHP built a SEPARATE message for the external-backend branch carrying no priority, and even once unified stored priority only INSIDE the message sub-document where a sort cannot reach, sorting on created_at alone. Ruby never WROTE the field its own dequeue read back (doc['priority'] || 0), and also sorted on created_at alone. Node's sort was RIGHT all along ({priority: -1, createdAt: 1}) but priority never ARRIVED - the QueueBackend interface had no such parameter and Queue.push passed it only to liteBackend, so the sort ordered on a field no document carried. Python was already correct and is the reference. MONGODB now stores priority top-level and sorts highest-first with ties oldest-first, matching the file backend's policy. RABBITMQ and KAFKA RAISE naming the backend and the operation (invariant 6): a RabbitMQ queue is FIFO and native priority needs the queue DECLARED with x-max-priority, which an existing queue cannot be redeclared with (PRECONDITION_FAILED), so enabling it would break every queue already in service; Kafka has no priority concept at all. Node satisfies that half by refusing both backends at construction (ADR-0022). Mutation-proved in all four: reverting each framework's fix kills exactly 'a higher priority job is delivered before an older lower priority one', and removing a refusal guard kills exactly the refusal case.

invariants.rule: A backend that genuinely cannot perform an operation RAISES, naming the backend and the operation. It may never silently no-op or return an empty result that is indistinguishable from success.
invariants.why: ADR-0024 rule 3: a method that exists and no-ops is worse than one that is absent, because absent fails loudly at the call site. Every silent-no-op finding in this subsystem would have been caught on the first run if this rule held.
cases: an unknown queue backend raises instead of silently using file
a queue backend name is normalised before it is resolved
the guard still accepts every documented backend name
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four. The BACKEND-SELECTION half closed 2026-08-03: an unrecognised TINA4_QUEUE_BACKEND now RAISES naming the value and the valid set in all four (php + nodejs previously fell through to the local file store), and the name is normalised in all four (ruby previously normalised only the env var, so an explicit backend: 'FILE' raised). The per-OPERATION half closed 2026-08-04: php failed(), retryFailed() and deadLetters() were FATAL with 'Call to undefined method' on rabbitmq and kafka, because the two broker backends simply did not define them. All three are now DECLARED ON THE QueueBackend INTERFACE, so the type system enforces their presence permanently rather than a test catching each new backend later, and both brokers implement them as refusals naming the backend and the operation and explaining what to use instead. They are not empty lists: an empty list would claim nothing has failed, which ADR-0022 decision 7 forbids. Ruby's five remaining guards became refuse_operation! in the same pass.

invariants.rule: close() exists on the top-level Queue in every framework and releases whatever the configured backend holds. It is idempotent - closing twice is safe - and closing a file-backed queue is not an error.
invariants.why: ADR-0024's swap test applies to shutdown, not just to work: if close() releases a Mongo client on one provider and throws on another, the same application shutdown code cannot survive changing one env var. A long-lived process that never releases a broker connection leaks it, and a guarded caller that probes respond_to?(:close) silently skips a backend that lacks the method - so an ABSENT close is indistinguishable from a close that did nothing.
cases: closing a queue releases the backend connection
closing a queue twice is safe
closing a file backed queue is not an error
invariants.status: PROVEN in all four 2026-08-04 on the lab (Ubuntu 24.04.4) against a live MongoDB, RabbitMQ and Kafka, with TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES=1. PHP already had close() on the interface and on all four backends; only the top-level Queue::close() was missing, so the last inch was the whole defect. Python gained close() on the Queue and on all four adapters. Node gained it on the Queue, on liteBackend and on mongoBackend, and close() is now a REQUIRED member of QueueBackendInterface, mirroring PHP so the type system holds the line. Two further defects surfaced in Ruby while doing it: close was NOT IDEMPOTENT (a second call raised Bunny::ChannelAlreadyClosed: cannot use a closed channel, measured directly, now fixed with ensure-nil on rabbitmq and kafka), and LiteBackend had no close AT ALL - so every respond_to?(:close) guard in the tree silently skipped the DEFAULT backend, which is the one most installations run. Mutation-proved in all four: deleting Queue.close() turns the suite red at the call site, and making close() delegate nowhere fails on the retained handles by name (for example ['_producer','_consumer'] still held). Node's close() releases nothing today by design and says so in code: per ADR-0022 its Mongo backend spawns a child process per operation which closes its own client, so a handle assertion there would be theatre.
